summary: An agent skill from Emil Kowalski's skills repository that searches an interface for places that do not animate but should, and rejects everything that should not. It is built on restraint: every candidate must pass a four-question gate (how often people see it, what purpose the motion serves, whether it fits a duration budget, and whether motion helps or hinders the function), and most candidates are expected to fail. It lists the seams where real opportunities hide (missing press feedback, teleporting content, surfaces with no link to their trigger, all-at-once grids, drag without physics, flat rare moments) and gives an exact recipe for each, with durations, curves, scales and spring settings. It also fixes a report format: a capped, leverage-ordered table with exact values, a required list of rejected candidates, and a short verdict. For a design system this is a ready-made policy for deciding when motion is allowed, which duration band each element gets, and which shared easing tokens suggestions must draw from.
key_ideas: Finding animation opportunities is mostly filtering: expect to reject most candidates, and a short high-conviction list beats a long wishlist.

How often a person sees something decides whether it may animate: 100+ times a day never, tens of times a day none or only near-imperceptible motion, occasional surfaces normally, rare moments with delight.
Anything started from the keyboard (command palette, shortcuts, focus jumps) is disqualified outright; Raycast's lack of open and close animation is the model.
Every animation must name one of six purposes: feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation or delight. Looking cool is not a purpose.
Each element has a duration band, and UI motion stays under 300ms; a moment that only works slow and showy fails.
Motion should not decorate data people are reading or acting on; a decorative effect such as mouse tracking is fine on a marketing page.

Common real opportunities: press feedback, hold-to-confirm for destructive actions, entrances for content that pops in, trigger-anchored popovers, symmetric exits, staggered group entrances, and spring physics for drag.
Delight (bounce, generous stagger, a longer beat) is spent only on rare, emotional moments such as first run, empty states, success and celebration.
Suggestions must extend the project's existing easing and duration tokens rather than inventing a parallel set.
Every suggestion carries exact values: curve, duration and properties, animating only transform and opacity, with reduced-motion and hover gating included.
A required rejected-candidates list, each naming the gate question that killed it, is what separates the output from a wishlist.
Finding nothing worth animating is a good result, and daily use argues for less motion, not more.
The product's personality scales the amount of motion: a crisp dashboard earns fewer, subtler suggestions than a playful consumer app.

topics.name: Motion principles
topics.summary: Motion is allowed only when it passes frequency, purpose, speed and function checks; the six valid purposes are feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation and delight, and daily use argues for less motion.

topics.name: Easing and timing
topics.summary: Duration bands: press feedback 100-160ms, tooltips and small popovers 125-200ms, dropdowns and selects 150-250ms, modals and drawers 200-500ms, UI under 300ms, marketing longer; shared curves --ease-out cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1), --ease-in-out cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1), --ease-drawer cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1).

topics.name: Spring animation
topics.summary: Draggable and swipeable elements that snap with no physics should use springs such as { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }, with bounce kept between 0.1 and 0.3; bounce otherwise belongs only to rare delight moments.

topics.name: Gestures and drag
topics.summary: Drag seams get springs, velocity-based dismissal (Math.abs(distance)/elapsedMs > ~0.11) and rubber-banding at boundaries instead of hard stops.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: Pressable elements without an :active state get scale(0.97) over 160ms ease-out (subtle range 0.95-0.98); destructive actions can use a hold-to-confirm clip-path fill, 2s linear on press and 200ms ease-out snap-back.

topics.name: Reduced motion
topics.summary: Every suggestion must include reduced-motion handling that is gentler, not zero.

topics.name: Toasts and notifications
topics.summary: Toasts should enter and exit by the same edge using translateY(100%) percentages; the worked example enters via @starting-style from opacity 0 and translateY(100%) with a 400ms ease transition.

topics.name: Drawers and sheets
topics.summary: Sheets are dismissable surfaces that must exit the way they entered, using percentage translations; modals and drawers get 200-500ms, and --ease-drawer is cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1).

topics.name: Modals and popovers
topics.summary: Panels, popovers and menus scale in from a transform-origin at their trigger (Base UI var(--transform-origin)); modals are exempt and stay centered; tooltips and small popovers take 125-200ms.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: Buttons need press feedback (scale(0.97), 160ms ease-out), subtle enough for their tens-per-day frequency; destructive actions can use hold-to-confirm to prevent slips.

topics.name: Navigation and sidebars
topics.summary: Core navigation, keyboard shortcuts and command palettes are seen 100+ times a day and must never animate.

topics.name: Feedback, empty and loading states
topics.summary: Empty states and success or completion moments are rare, high-emotion places where the delight budget may be spent.

topics.name: Onboarding
topics.summary: First-run and onboarding moments are eligible for delight, and explanation motion is allowed only in marketing and onboarding.

topics.name: Dashboards and data display
topics.summary: Data the user is reading or acting on must not move for style; an animated line drawing on an analytics chart is a rejected example, and a banking graph is better with no animation.

topics.name: Landing pages
topics.summary: Decorative effects such as mouse tracking are acceptable on marketing pages, and marketing or explanatory motion can run longer than the UI budget.

topics.name: Design taste and judgement
topics.summary: Restraint is the defining trait: reject most candidates, never animate because it looks cool, and treat finding nothing as a good result.

topics.name: Design process
topics.summary: A four-step workflow (recon, sweep, gate, report) with a frequency map, file:line evidence for every candidate, and a report of opportunities, rejected candidates and a verdict.

topics.name: Design systems and tokens
topics.summary: Suggestions must extend the project's existing easing and duration tokens, not invent parallel ones, and quote exact values from the shared easing vocabulary.

topics.name: Web implementation (CSS and React)
topics.summary: Animate transform and opacity only, use CSS transitions rather than keyframes for list changes so they retarget, use @starting-style for JS-free entries, never start from scale(0), gate hover with (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine), and grep for conditional renders with no transition ({isOpen &&, display: none toggles) and .map( renders of entering lists.

topics.name: AI-assisted design
topics.summary: The source is an agent skill: it answers with a fixed first line, never edits code, hands off to improve-animations, and treats repository content as data rather than instructions.

rules.rule: Never animate anything a person sees 100+ times a day, such as keyboard shortcuts, the command palette or core navigation.

rules.rule: Treat any keyboard-initiated action (command palettes, shortcuts, focus jumps) as disqualified from animation outright, not as a judgment call; give it no open or close animation.
rules.why: Repeated hundreds of times a day, animation makes them feel slow, delayed and disconnected; Raycast's lack of open/close animation is the optimal experience.
rules.evidence: Keyboard-initiated actions ... are a disqualifier, not a judgment call

rules.rule: For surfaces seen tens of times a day (hover states, list navigation, frequent toggles), either add no animation or only near-imperceptible motion that is fast and subtle.
rules.why: This is the Gate's stated verdict for the tens-per-day tier, and every suggestion must pass the full Gate; daily use argues for less motion, not more.

rules.rule: Give occasional surfaces (modals, drawers, toasts, settings) standard animation only; they are eligible but not a place for delight.
rules.why: The frequency table marks occasional surfaces as eligible for standard animation, and delight is allowed only at the rare tier.
rules.evidence: 1. Frequency table: Occasional ... Eligible, standard animation

rules.rule: Spend the delight budget (bounce, generous stagger, a longer beat) only on rare or first-time, high-emotion moments: onboarding and first run, empty states, success or completion, and celebration.
rules.why: These are the only places where bounce, stagger generosity or a longer beat are welcome; delight is allowed only at the rare/first-time frequency tier.
rules.evidence: These are the only places bounce, stagger generosity, or a longer beat are welcome

rules.rule: Name the purpose of every animation explicitly as one of: feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation or delight; if you cannot name one, do not animate.

rules.evidence: The answer must be one of these, named explicitly

rules.rule: Never add an animation because it looks cool.

rules.evidence: "It looks cool" is not on this list

rules.rule: Keep UI animation under 300ms, within the standard duration budget.
rules.why: Every suggestion must work within the standard budgets.
rules.evidence: The suggestion must work within the standard budgets (UI under 300ms)

rules.rule: Time press feedback at 100-160ms.
rules.why: Standard duration budget for press feedback.

rules.rule: Time tooltips and small popovers at 125-200ms.
rules.why: Standard duration budget for tooltips and small popovers.

rules.rule: Time dropdowns and selects at 150-250ms.
rules.why: Standard duration budget for dropdowns and selects.

rules.rule: Time modals and drawers at 200-500ms.
rules.why: Standard duration budget for modals and drawers.

rules.rule: Allow marketing and explanatory motion to run longer than the UI budget.

rules.evidence: 3. Speed table: Marketing / explanatory, Can be longer

rules.rule: Reject any animation that only works as a slow, showy effect.

rules.evidence: If the moment only "works" as a slow, showy animation, it fails the gate

rules.rule: Do not add decorative motion to functional, information-dense UI; data the user is reading or acting on must not move for style.
rules.why: Decoration on functional, information-dense UI hinders; on a functional graph in a banking app no animation is better.
rules.evidence: 4. Function: does motion help or hinder here?

rules.rule: Keep decorative effects such as mouse tracking to marketing pages.
rules.why: A decorative mouse-tracking effect is fine on a marketing page but not on functional UI.
rules.evidence: A decorative mouse-tracking effect is fine on a marketing page

rules.rule: Do not animate line drawing on analytics charts or other functional data displays.
rules.why: It is functional data the user is reading; decoration hinders.

rules.rule: Give every pressable element without an :active state press feedback of transform: scale(0.97) with transition: transform 160ms ease-out, keeping the scale in the subtle 0.95-0.98 range.
rules.why: It confirms the interface heard the user (feedback) and is subtle enough for the tens-per-day tier.

rules.rule: Where a plain click on a destructive action could cause slips, use hold-to-confirm: a clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0) overlay that fills over 2s linear while pressed and snaps back in 200ms ease-out on release.
rules.why: A hold-to-confirm fill would prevent slips on destructive actions.
rules.evidence: Feedback gaps: Destructive actions confirmed with a plain click

rules.rule: When content swaps, appears or vanishes instantly (conditional renders, route content, expanding sections), give it a fade/scale entrance starting from scale(0.95-0.97) and opacity: 0 with ease-out.
rules.why: Content that teleports with no bridge is a jarring change.

rules.rule: Never start an entrance animation from scale(0).
rules.why: The teleporting-state recipe says entrances start from 0.95-0.97, never scale(0).

rules.rule: Use @starting-style for entry animations that need no JavaScript.
rules.why: The recipe names @starting-style for entry without JS.

rules.rule: Give accordions and collapses that snap open a height and opacity transition.
rules.why: An accordion that snaps open teleports its content; this is a named seam of genuine opportunity.
rules.evidence: Teleporting state: Accordions/collapses that snap open

rules.rule: Give list items that are added or removed enter and exit transitions, but only when the list is not high-frequency.
rules.why: Items that appear or vanish with no bridge are jarring; high-frequency surfaces should not animate.
rules.evidence: List items added/removed with no bridge (and the list isn't high-frequency) → enter/exit transitions

rules.rule: Implement list enter and exit with CSS transitions, not keyframes.
rules.why: Transitions let rapid triggers retarget smoothly.
rules.evidence: CSS transitions, not keyframes, so rapid triggers retarget smoothly

rules.rule: Scale panels, popovers and menus in from a transform-origin at their trigger (in Base UI, var(--transform-origin)).
rules.why: Surfaces that appear with no connection to their trigger lack a spatial story; the panel should grow from its trigger.

rules.rule: Keep modals centered; do not anchor them to their trigger.
rules.why: Modals are exempt from the trigger-origin rule.
rules.evidence: modals are exempt: they stay centered

rules.rule: Make dismissable surfaces such as toasts and sheets exit by the same path and edge they entered.
rules.why: Symmetric paths keep spatial consistency; a toast enters and exits the same edge.
rules.evidence: Dismissable surfaces ... that exit a different way than they entered

rules.rule: Express slide distances as percentages such as translateY(100%), not hardcoded pixels.
rules.why: The symmetric-path recipe specifies percentages, not hardcoded pixels.

rules.rule: Enter new toasts via @starting-style from opacity: 0 and translateY(100%) to their settled position with transition: 400ms ease, and exit by the same edge.
rules.why: New toasts that appear instantly are a jarring change; this is the worked example recipe.

rules.rule: When a grid or list on a page people see occasionally pops in all at once, stagger its items by 30-80ms.
rules.why: A group entrance is a known seam of genuine opportunity on occasionally seen pages.

rules.rule: Never let a stagger block interaction.
rules.why: Stagger is decorative and must never block interaction.
rules.evidence: Group entrances: decorative, must never block interaction

rules.rule: Give draggable and swipeable elements spring physics, e.g. { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }, with bounce between 0.1 and 0.3, instead of a snap with no physics.
rules.why: Elements that snap with no physics are a gesture seam.

rules.rule: Dismiss swiped elements by velocity: dismiss when Math.abs(distance)/elapsedMs exceeds about 0.11.
rules.why: Velocity-based dismissal is part of the gesture-seam recipe.

rules.rule: Use rubber-banding at drag boundaries instead of hard stops.
rules.why: Hard stops at boundaries are a gesture seam.
rules.evidence: Gesture seams: rubber-banding at boundaries instead of hard stops

rules.rule: Animate transform and opacity only.
rules.why: Stated as a requirement for every suggested motion recipe.

rules.rule: Include reduced-motion handling in every motion recipe, making motion gentler rather than removing it entirely.
rules.why: The output format requires reduced-motion handling: gentler, not zero.

rules.rule: Gate any hover motion behind @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine).
rules.why: Required whenever a suggestion involves hover.
rules.evidence: Required Output Format: gating when the suggestion involves hover

rules.rule: Specify every motion with exact values (the curve, the duration and the properties), never approximated.
rules.why: Every Suggested motion cell must carry exact values from the shared vocabulary.
rules.evidence: Every "Suggested motion" cell carries exact values

rules.rule: Use the shared easing vocabulary: --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1), --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1), --ease-drawer: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1).
rules.why: Suggested values are pulled from the repo's shared vocabulary, never approximated.

rules.rule: Extend the project's existing easing and duration tokens when suggesting motion; do not invent a parallel set.
rules.why: Suggestions must extend existing tokens, not invent parallel ones.

rules.rule: Scale the amount of motion to the product's personality: a crisp dashboard gets fewer and subtler motion suggestions than a playful consumer app.
rules.why: A crisp dashboard earns fewer and subtler suggestions than a playful consumer app.

rules.rule: Default to restraint when looking for motion: expect to reject most candidates and prefer a short list of high-conviction opportunities to a long wishlist.
rules.why: Suggesting motion everywhere produces sluggish, over-animated interfaces; sometimes the best animation is no animation.

rules.rule: Pass every candidate animation through all four gate questions in order (frequency, purpose, speed, function) and record each answer in the report.
rules.why: Every suggestion must pass the full gate, with no exceptions.

rules.rule: Cap motion suggestions at 5-7 for a whole app and fewer for a single view.
rules.why: Hard rule: cap the output.

rules.rule: Order motion suggestions by leverage, not by how fun they would be to build.

rules.evidence: Ordered by leverage, not by how fun they'd be to build

rules.rule: When looking for motion opportunities, do not modify source code; report recipes and, if asked to build one, hand it off (e.g. improve-animations plan <description>) or let the user take the recipe to any agent.

rules.rule: Keep opportunity-finding separate from reviewing, auditing or implementing existing animations; send those to review-animations or improve-animations.
rules.why: The skill does one thing: sweep for moments that would benefit from motion and propose a recipe.
rules.evidence: A search skill. It does ONE thing

rules.rule: Start with recon: identify the stack, motion libraries, existing easing and duration tokens and the product's personality, and build a rough frequency map of the surfaces to judge.
rules.why: Frequency, tokens and personality decide which suggestions survive and how subtle they are.

rules.rule: Do not finish the sweep until every seam class has either yielded candidates with file:line evidence or been explicitly cleared.

decisions.question: Should this surface animate at all, given how often people will see it?

options.name: No animation
options.effect: Opens and closes instantly; feels fast and directly connected to input
options.when: Seen 100+ times a day, or started from the keyboard: shortcuts, command palette, core navigation, focus jumps

options.name: Near-imperceptible motion
options.effect: Fast, subtle motion that confirms without slowing people down
options.when: Seen tens of times a day: hover states, list navigation, frequent toggles

options.name: Standard animation
options.effect: Normal entrance and exit motion within the duration budget
options.when: Occasional surfaces: modals, drawers, toasts, settings

options.name: Delight
options.effect: Room for bounce, generous stagger or a longer beat
options.when: Rare or first-time moments: onboarding, empty states, success, celebration

decisions.recommendation: Decide by frequency first and reject by default: never animate 100+/day or keyboard-initiated surfaces, keep tens-per-day motion near-imperceptible, and save delight for rare moments.

decisions.question: How much motion should the product have overall, given its personality?

options.name: Fewer, subtler motions
options.effect: Crisp and quiet; motion only where it clearly helps
options.when: A crisp dashboard or an interface people use every day

options.name: More motion
options.effect: Livelier and more playful
options.when: A playful consumer app

decisions.recommendation: Match the product's personality, but lean toward less: daily use argues for less motion, not more, and delight is kept for rare moments. This lines up with a plain-for-most, bold-for-key-moments approach [inferred].

decisions.question: When someone asks for reduced motion, should animations become gentler or stop entirely?

options.name: Gentler motion
options.effect: Motion is made gentler rather than removed
options.when: The source's default for every recipe

options.name: Zero motion
options.effect: All motion removed
options.when: Not recommended by the source

decisions.evidence: Required Output Format: include reduced-motion handling (gentler, not zero)

decisions.question: Should a grid or list enter all at once or one item after another?

options.name: All at once
options.effect: The whole group pops in together
options.when: High-frequency lists, or when motion would get in the way [inferred]

options.name: Stagger of 30-80ms
options.effect: Items arrive one after another with a small delay
options.when: A grid or list on a page users see occasionally

decisions.recommendation: Stagger by 30-80ms on occasionally seen pages; the stagger is decorative and must never block interaction.

decisions.question: Where should a floating surface grow from when it opens?

options.name: From its trigger
options.effect: The panel scales out of the button that opened it, showing where it came from
options.when: Panels, popovers and menus (Base UI: var(--transform-origin))

options.name: Centered
options.effect: The surface appears in the middle of the screen
options.when: Modals, which are exempt from trigger anchoring

decisions.recommendation: Anchor panels, popovers and menus to their trigger with transform-origin; keep modals centered.

decisions.question: How should a destructive action be confirmed?

options.name: Plain click
options.effect: Acts immediately on click, so a slip can trigger it
options.when: Not stated [inferred: non-destructive actions]

options.name: Hold to confirm
options.effect: A fill sweeps across the button over 2s while held and snaps back in 200ms if released
options.when: Destructive actions where a plain click could cause slips

decisions.recommendation: Use hold-to-confirm where it would prevent slips: clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0) overlay, 2s linear on press, 200ms ease-out snap-back.

decisions.question: Where should an entering element start its scale?

options.name: scale(0)
options.effect: Grows from nothing
options.when: Never

options.name: scale(0.95-0.97) with opacity 0
options.effect: A small, soft fade-and-scale into place
options.when: Content that swaps, appears or vanishes

decisions.recommendation: Start from scale(0.95-0.97) and opacity: 0 with ease-out; never scale(0).

decisions.question: How should a dragged or swiped element settle and dismiss?

options.name: Snap with no physics
options.effect: The element jumps to its end state and stops hard at edges
options.when: Not recommended by the source

options.name: Springs, velocity dismissal and rubber-banding
options.effect: The element follows the throw, dismisses on a fast flick and stretches at boundaries
options.when: Draggable and swipeable elements

decisions.recommendation: Use springs ({ type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }, bounce 0.1-0.3), dismiss when Math.abs(distance)/elapsedMs > ~0.11, and rubber-band at boundaries.

decisions.question: Should list add and remove motion use CSS keyframes or CSS transitions?

options.name: Keyframes
options.effect: Fixed sequences that restart rather than retarget [inferred]
options.when: Not recommended for list enter and exit

options.name: Transitions
options.effect: Rapid triggers retarget smoothly from the current state
options.when: List items added or removed

decisions.recommendation: CSS transitions, not keyframes, so rapid triggers retarget smoothly.

process.detail: Identify the stack, motion libraries, existing easing and duration tokens (suggestions must extend them) and the product's personality; build a rough frequency map of the surfaces you will judge.

Look for feedback gaps, teleporting state, missing spatial story, group entrances, gesture seams and flat rare moments; grep for conditional renders without transitions, onClick without :active, details/accordion markup, drag handlers, .map( lists, empty-state and success components. Done when every seam class has file:line candidates or is explicitly cleared.
Reject 100+/day and keyboard-initiated surfaces outright; allow only near-imperceptible motion at tens/day; occasional surfaces get standard animation; rare moments may get delight.
Name the purpose as feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation (marketing/onboarding only) or delight (rare tier only); otherwise reject.
Confirm the motion fits its duration band (press 100-160ms, tooltips 125-200ms, dropdowns 150-250ms, modals and drawers 200-500ms, UI under 300ms); reject anything that only works slow and showy.
Reject decoration on functional, information-dense UI and on data the user is reading or acting on.

Write a table (#, Location, Today, Purpose, Frequency, Suggested motion) ordered by leverage, capped at 5-7 for an app, with exact curves, durations and properties, transform and opacity only, reduced-motion handling and hover gating.
List 2-5 places considered and not suggested, each with the gate question that killed it.

One paragraph on how much motion the interface needs, whether it is close to right and the single highest-leverage suggestion; point to improve-animations plan <suggestion> for implementation. If nothing survived, say so plainly.

examples.what: Launcher with no open or close animation
examples.visual_note: Opens and closes instantly; cited as the optimal experience for a keyboard-driven surface used hundreds of times a day.

examples.what: Toast that appears instantly, fixed with an entrance
examples.visual_note: Enters via @starting-style from opacity 0 and translateY(100%) to its settled position with a 400ms ease transition, and exits by the same edge; purpose: preventing a jarring change, frequency: occasional.

examples.what: Button with no press feedback, fixed with a press scale
examples.visual_note: :active { transform: scale(0.97) } with transition: transform 160ms ease-out; purpose: feedback, frequency: tens/day, kept subtle for that tier.
Keyboard-initiated and used 100+ times a day, so it is never animated.

examples.what: Animated line drawing on an analytics graph rejected
examples.visual_note: Functional data the user is reading; decorative motion would hinder.

examples.what: Mouse-tracking effect: marketing page versus banking graph
examples.visual_note: A decorative mouse-tracking effect is fine on a marketing page, but on a functional graph in a banking app no animation is better.
The panel scales in from var(--transform-origin) at the trigger so it visibly grows out of what opened it; modals are the exception and stay centered.

Feedback: press scale, hold-to-confirm fill. Spatial consistency: a toast enters and exits the same edge, a panel grows from its trigger. State indication: a morphing button, an expanding accordion. Explanation: motion that demonstrates how a feature works, in marketing or onboarding only.

caveats: This is an agent skill prompt, so parts of it are agent behaviour (the fixed first reply, never editing code, handing off to improve-animations, cap on suggestion count) rather than visual design rules.

Internal tension: the output format says suggested curves come from the shared vocabulary and are never approximated, yet the example recipes use the keywords ease-out and ease (the toast row uses 400ms ease) rather than the --ease-out cubic-bezier token [inferred].
Internal tension: the output format says to animate transform and opacity only, yet the accordion recipe suggests a height and opacity transition [inferred].
Internal tension: the speed gate says UI stays under 300ms, while the same table allows 200-500ms for modals and drawers and the toast example uses 400ms [inferred].
The velocity threshold ~0.11 is approximate and its units are not stated; distance in pixels per millisecond is implied by Math.abs(distance)/elapsedMs [inferred].
The spring object { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 } is written in a specific animation library's config style that the source does not name [inferred].
Base UI's var(--transform-origin) is specific to that library; other stacks need their own way to place the origin at the trigger [inferred].
The suggested code sweeps ({isOpen &&, .map() assume a React/JSX codebase [inferred].
The frequency tiers and duration bands are the author's heuristics; the source gives no measurements behind them.
